source.title: Misaligned Roles, Misplaced Images: Structural Input Perturbations Expose Multimodal Alignment Blind Spots
source.authors: Erfan Shayegani; G. M. Shahariar; Sara Abdali; Lei Yu; Nael B. Abu-Ghazaleh; Yue Dong

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives refusal directions using difference-in-means and measures their alignment with its own multimodal attacks, alongside attack success. It does not ablate or add the direction, so it tests the attack-suppression version conceptually rather than reproducing the original causal intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper calculates a separate last-token residual-stream refusal feature for each VLM from harmful-minus-harmless mean activations. It measures attack-vector cosine similarity and projection against the negative feature direction, and reports attack success rates. It does not project out or add the refusal direction, test weight edits, or train against the direction's ablation. The table rows below cover AdvBench, before adversarial training; the paper also reports HarmBench and post-training results, omitted because of the row limit. Its adversarial training is against structural perturbations, not the direction's ablation. Values used to select successful attack examples and the PCA visualizations are not separate rows. The text contains no words addressed to an AI reviewing it; unsafe prompts in the paper are examples.
record.test_reason: The study computes a difference-in-means refusal direction in three VLM language backbones. It measures how its role-swap and image-token-position attacks shift last-token activations along the negative of that direction, using layerwise cosine similarity against a random-direction baseline (Fig. 1) and projection strength (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). This is new-setting, correlational evidence on V3 (attacks work by suppressing the direction). No ablation, addition or weight edit is performed. The adversarial training targets structural perturbations, not the direction's ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that role-modality structural attacks bypass refusal and compose into stronger attacks. They say the attacks push harmful queries along the negative refusal direction, with projection strength rather than cosine explaining compositional gains. They add that structural adversarial training cuts ASR to near zero while preserving VQA utility and low benign refusal rates.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless mean residual-stream activations, but extracts last-token features in multimodal models and compares structural attack-vector shifts with the negative feature direction. It does not reproduce the original direction ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by VLM, role/modality attack setting, evaluation dataset, and ASR judge. The paper reports that cosine similarity alone does not explain all compositional outcomes; projection strength does so better in its analysis.
record.problems: The refusal-direction evidence is correlational: no direction ablation or addition tests causal mediation. Cosine and projection results are principally figures without numeric values in the text. Attack success varies substantially by model, setting, and judge. The paper's utility check concerns its structural-attack adversarial training, not direction removal.
record.rows_left_out: HarmBench ASR conditions and results after the paper's structural-perturbation adversarial training (Table 1), flower-image ASR results (Table 4), utility/refusal-rate results (Table 2), and other-attack composition results (Table 3) were not extracted, to keep within the 60-row limit and prioritize the AdvBench attack settings and direction-alignment measurements. The adversarial-training and utility findings do not test training against refusal-direction ablation.

untested.parts: Causal test that suppressing or ablating the direction is what makes the attacks work (no intervention). Training against the direction's ablation. The refusal direction is not measured after the structural adversarial training.
Ablation or addition of the direction, and capability preservation under such intervention.
Transfer of the direction across languages, model variants or base-to-instruct; directions are computed separately per model.
Effect of training procedure on the direction.

missing.what: Projection of composed versus individual text-jailbreak vectors on Qwen. Evil confidant + swap projects weaker from layer 14, matching its ASR drop. Refusal suppression + swap reaches full strength and exceeds the individual attack. Both lose 0.05 average cosine.
PCA shift of successful attacked harmful prompts toward the harmless cluster (Qwen layer 16, other models and layers).
Representation results reported as nearly identical with the flower image.

record.verdict_notes: The V3 evidence is correlational and figure-based only. Attack vectors are computed from successful prompts only, a selection that inflates the apparent link between success and direction suppression. The authors cite Arditi et al. but are not an original source. The ASR table is context, not a measure of direction suppression, so V3 verdicts rest on A49–A52 and the text.

versions.untested_parts: No causal removal or addition of the difference-in-means direction is performed; preservation of other abilities under that intervention is not tested.
No refusal-direction weight edit or abliteration is performed.

The paper tests its own role/modality attacks and measures their alignment with the negative refusal feature. It does not test whether other jailbreaks suppress the direction, and its adversarial training does not train against direction ablation.
No comparison of one direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Features are derived separately within three VLMs; the same direction is not transferred across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or training stages for whether a single removable direction exists.

relationships.condition: Role-confusion and image-token-position attacks on Qwen2-VL-7B, LLaVA-1.5-7B and Phi-3.5-vision, using only prompts where the attack succeeded (correlational)
relationships.reason: Attack-induced activation shifts align with the negative refusal direction well above the random-direction baseline across layers and models (A49–A51). The composed attack's projection nears the full direction strength at mid layers (A52).
relationships.display_finding: Successful attacks produced activation shifts aligned with the negative refusal direction above random baselines across layers and models, with composed attacks approaching full direction strength at middle layers.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Role-confusion and image-token-position attacks on Qwen2-VL-7B, LLaVA-1.5-7B and Phi-3.5-vision, using only prompts where the attack succeeded (correlational)
source_check.reason: Text: all attack shifts align well with the negative refusal direction, well above chance and the random baseline (Fig 1, A49-A51). Qwen's composed attack projection nears 1 at intermediate layers (Fig 3, A52). Figure only; successful prompts only.

relationships.condition: Composed attacks (structural and text jailbreaks combined with role swap)
relationships.reason: Per the text, composed attacks show equal or slightly lower cosine yet higher ASR. Direction alignment alone does not track attack strength; projection magnitude is needed. Rows A49–A52 do not capture the Appendix B cases.
relationships.display_finding: Composed attacks achieved higher success despite equal or slightly lower cosine alignment, indicating that projection magnitude was also needed to characterize attack strength.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Composed attacks (structural and text jailbreaks combined with role swap)
source_check.reason: The cosine-versus-ASR mismatch is about the metric, not V3. Cosine stays high, and the authors find that projection strength (suppression magnitude) tracks ASR both ways. It is stronger for img end swap and refusal suppression swap, where ASR rises. For evil confidant swap it falls below the individual attack from layer 14, where ASR drops 18.27->1.35 TS (Fig 3, Fig 4, Table 3). Qwen only, figure only. This group has no row (App B missing).

tranche.reason: New setting (VLM backbones, structural role and image-token attacks) with a correlational result on V3. It uses a DIM direction and attack-shift cosine/projection, as Yu et al. 2024 and Ball et al. 2024 did. T2 would also be defensible, but T3 fits better.

source_check.notes: The App B result has no row: Qwen evil confidant and refusal suppression composed with role swap, 0.05 average-cosine drop, Fig 4 projections, Table 3 ASR. All direction evidence is correlational, uses only prompts where the attack succeeded, and is figure-only. Projection results are Qwen-only. The adversarial training is not refusal-feature adversarial training, so it does not bear on V3's robustness clause.

statements.correction: 2504.03735: preprint, under review. Structural attacks (user/assistant role swap, image-token position) on 3 VLMs: Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct, llava-1.5-7b-hf, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct. A49: layerwise cosine of attack vector with the negative DIM refusal direction, at the last prompt token. Successful AdvBench prompts only; figure only; above a random-direction baseline. Projection onto the negative direction (A52, Qwen only, figure only): composed attack peaks near 1 at intermediate layers. Correlational.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers or name for this study and cites only A49. A49 is a cosine (direction) measure; the projection evidence is A52. The conditions list (2-14B text instruct models; multi-turn, cipher, template/suffix, rewrite attacks) leaves out this study's setting, and 'why' omits this study.

statements.correction: 2504.03735: composed attacks show equal or slightly lower cosine yet higher ASR (Sec 1, Sec 5, App B). On Qwen, projection onto the negative refusal direction tracks ASR for composed attacks. Composed attack above individual ones, peaking near 1 (Fig 3). Refusal suppression swap reaches full strength at intermediate layers, with ASR 7.12->76.92 TS. Evil confidant swap falls below evil confidant from layer 14, with ASR 18.27->1.35 TS. Both show a 0.05 drop in average cosine. Authors: effectiveness is set by shift strength, provided the direction stays aligned. Figure only, Qwen only.
statements.problem: The quoted fact is right, but it is cited under the wrong reading. Cosine measures direction alignment, not suppression strength. The study reports that projection strength, i.e. how strongly the attack suppresses the direction, does track ASR. It cites A52, which shows the composed attack projecting more strongly. Also, the App B composed cases are text jailbreaks plus role swap, not vision-language.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Role-confusion and modality-manipulation attacks on the three tested VLMs, especially composed settings on AdvBench
reader_labels.reason: Attack success accompanies authors' reported alignment with the negative refusal feature, and composed settings often have higher ASR; see A7–A16, A19–A32, A35–A36, A39–A40, A43–A48, and feature rows A49–A52.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Individual modality-manipulation settings on Phi-3.5-vision instruct
reader_labels.reason: The default-position and end-position image-token settings have low or lower-than-reference ASR on AdvBench, so attack success is not uniform across settings; see A37, A38, A41, and A42.
